Sunday, 12 March 2034, six in the morning. The music teacher from Corte calls Julien. Antoine, the old shepherd who watered the burnt lime tree, died during the night. The teacher tells him what Antoine said on his last day.
Julien, it’s me. I’m sorry to call you so early. Antoine left us last night.
Oh no… Did he suffer?
No. He went in his sleep. Yesterday evening, Marie-Ange told me he was calm and had eaten well.
Did he say anything, before?
Yes. Yesterday afternoon he asked to see the mayor. He told him he wanted to be buried in the little cemetery, where you can see the square.
That doesn’t surprise me. He never wanted to leave his tree.
He added that he didn’t want flowers. He asked for everyone to bring a glass of water for the lime tree.
That’s him all over. And the tree, how is it?
Still nothing. Just yesterday evening, Antoine asked whether the tree had buds. Marie-Ange told him no, that they would have to wait.
And what did he say?
He said he knew, and that it should be watered anyway. Then he said one last thing: that you should be told, and that the little girl would know what to do.
Rose-Hélène… She’ll want to come. When is the funeral?
Tuesday, at eleven. Antoine made me promise to tell you. He said she would come.
He was right. We’ll be there.

1. Reported speech: the reporting verb
Reported speech relays someone’s words without quotation marks, using a reporting verb. Vary your verbs: a good text doesn’t only use “dire”!
dire, affirmer, déclarer
a statement
expliquer, préciser, ajouter
an explanation, an extra detail
répondre, répliquer
an answer
demander, se demander
a question or a request
annoncer, avouer, promettre
news, a confession, a promise
If the reporting verb is in the PRESENT (“il dit que…”), the tenses don’t change: “Il dit qu’il viendra.” The sequence of tenses only applies after a verb in the PAST.
2. The sequence of tenses
After a reporting verb in the past (il a dit, il disait, il avait dit), the tenses “take a step back”:
present: « Je veux être enterré là. »
imperfect: Il a dit qu’il voulait être enterré là.
passé composé: « J’ai bien mangé. »
pluperfect: Il a dit qu’il avait bien mangé.
future: « J’arroserai jusqu’au bout. »
present conditional: Il a dit qu’il arroserait jusqu’au bout.
future perfect: « J’aurai fini. »
past conditional: Il a dit qu’il aurait fini.
imperfect / pluperfect / conditional
don’t change

Romanian does NOT apply the sequence of tenses: “A spus că VREA”, “a spus că VA UDA”. French applies it obligatorily: “Il a dit qu’il VOULAIT”, “qu’il ARROSERAIT”. It’s one of the most common mistakes Romanians make!
3. The imperative and requests
An order or a request becomes “de + infinitive” or “que + subjunctive”:
“Bring water!” → He asked us to bring water.
“Water it anyway!” → He said to water it anyway.
“Don’t cry.” → He asked us not to cry.
He asked for everyone to bring a glass of water. (que + subjunctive)
In the negative, “ne pas” goes BEFORE the infinitive: “de ne pas pleurer”, not “de pleurer pas”.
4. Indirect questions
« Est-ce que l’arbre a des bourgeons ? »
Il a demandé si l’arbre avait des bourgeons.
« Qu’est-ce que tu as dit ? »
Il a demandé ce que j’avais dit.
Il a demandé ce qui se passait.
« Quand est l’enterrement ? »
Il a demandé quand était l’enterrement.
« Où vas-tu ? »
Il m’a demandé où j’allais.
In an indirect question there is NO inversion and NO question mark: “Il a demandé où j’allais.” (not “où allais-je ?”). And “est-ce que” disappears completely.
5. References to time and place
When you report later, the references relate to the moment back then, not to today:

ici / maintenant
là / à ce moment-là

On Monday 2 January 2034, at eight in the morning, Ioana walked into Nathalie’s office for the first time as director of the firm. The office was empty. Nathalie had taken everything except one thing: in the middle of the table she had left a sheet of paper. Ioana picked it up. It was a handwritten list headed “What nobody told you”.

The list contained ten pieces of advice. Nathalie wrote that a good director arrived first and left last, but only in the first month. That you should always answer clients the same day, even just to say you would answer the next day. That the bank would call in March, and that there was no need to panic. And at point ten she had written: “Don’t keep this office. It’s too big for one person.”

Ioana followed all the advice except the last for a week. Then she understood what Nathalie had meant. Alone in the big office, she could no longer hear anything of the firm’s life. She no longer knew who was laughing, who was tired, who had a problem. The following Monday she had the director’s office turned into a meeting room, and set up her table in the open-plan office, between Hugo and Sophie.

Hugo asked her why she was leaving such a lovely office. Ioana replied that Nathalie had advised her to. Hugo said he didn’t know Nathalie had left instructions. Ioana smiled. She said Nathalie had left ten instructions, and she was sure the eleventh would arrive by post before the end of the month. She was right. The letter arrived on 27 January, from Brittany, where Nathalie had settled.

For Nathalie, to everyone’s surprise, had moved to Brittany, to a small harbour near Nantes, twenty minutes from Yves Le Goff’s house. She had explained to Ioana on the phone that she had always dreamt of living by the sea, and that Yves had promised to teach her to make galettes. Ioana had asked her whether that was the only reason. Nathalie had laughed. She had said that at sixty-four you no longer needed reasons.

The eleventh instruction fitted into one sentence, written on the back of a postcard of a Breton lighthouse: “Listen to your staff more than to your clients. Clients leave; staff stay, if you listen to them.” Ioana pinned it above her new table in the open-plan office, next to Nathalie’s old ruler. Hugo read the card. He said it was the best of the eleven instructions. Ioana replied that he only said so because he was staff.

Nathalie also sent photos. Her on the beach, in a yellow oilskin, in the rain. Her at a crêpe griddle, with Yves holding her hand to show her the movement. A failed galette, burnt at the edges, with the caption: “First attempt. Yves says it’s a start.” Then, two weeks later, a perfect galette, golden and round: “Twenty-third attempt. Yves says I could open a crêperie. I think he’s lying.”

As Nathalie had predicted, the bank called in March. Mr Perrin wanted to review the first-quarter accounts. Ioana went with Sophie, the accountant, and a thirty-page file. Mr Perrin read everything, slowly, in silence. Then he said the firm was doing well, and that he had rarely seen such a calm handover. Ioana thought of the tenth instruction. She hadn’t panicked.

Sorina had come back from Bucharest in mid-December, as planned. But in February she asked to see Ioana privately. She was red, embarrassed, and was twisting a ring round her finger. She admitted that she and Andrei had been together since Christmas. She asked whether it was a problem, since he was following the site on behalf of the Stan family. Ioana burst out laughing. She said Viorica had guessed as early as October.

Meanwhile, in Corsica, the winter was long. The music teacher from Corte called Julien every week with news of Antoine. At the beginning of January he said the old shepherd was better, that he had started going out again and spent his mornings on the bench next to the black tree. At the end of January he said Antoine no longer went out. That he stayed in bed, at the home of the youngest of the three singers, who was looking after him.

In February the teacher said that every morning Antoine asked whether the tree had buds. The women went to look, then came back to tell him no, not yet, it was too early. Antoine replied that he knew, he just wanted someone to go and look. Then he asked them to water it anyway. They watered it. They had got into the habit, the teacher said, of whistling the three notes as they poured the water, because Antoine had asked them to.

The music teacher’s name was Paul Santoni. He was fifty-five, had taught music at the Corte secondary school for thirty years, and had himself learnt polyphonic singing from Antoine as a child. It was he who had accompanied the planting of the lime tree in 2031. Since the fire, he had gone up to the village twice a week despite the difficult road. He said he owed Antoine that much.

In Lyon, Rose-Hélène was waiting for spring with an impatience that worried her parents a little. She had hung a calendar on her bedroom wall, on which she crossed off each day with a red cross. She had circled 21 March in green, because Mrs Chevalier had told her it was the first day of spring. Every evening she asked her father how many days were left. Julien told her. She counted on her fingers.

Meanwhile, at school, Mrs Chevalier had started teaching the top-section children their letters. Rose-Hélène worked with an application the teacher had never seen in a five-year-old. She wanted to be able to read before spring. When Mrs Chevalier asked her why she was in such a hurry, she replied that she had a letter to read all by herself. An important letter. She no longer wanted anyone to read it to her.

On 4 March she turned six. For her birthday she asked for only one thing: a boat ticket to Corsica. Julien and Ioana looked at each other. They had planned to go in April, during the Easter holidays. They told her so. Rose-Hélène asked whether they could go earlier. Julien explained that in the mountains trees didn’t put out leaves before April. She said she wanted to be there when it happened.

On 12 March, at six in the morning, Julien’s phone rang. It was the music teacher. His voice was calm, too calm. Julien understood before he even spoke. Antoine had died in the night, in his sleep, at the home of the youngest of the three women. He had been ninety-seven since January. He hadn’t suffered. The evening before, he had again asked whether the tree had buds.

The teacher told him the rest slowly. The day before, Antoine had asked to see the mayor. He had told him he wanted to be buried in the little cemetery above the village, from where you could see the square. He had said he didn’t want flowers but water: that everyone who came to the funeral should bring a glass of water for the tree. And he had said that the little girl in Lyon should be told. That she would know what to do.

Julien hung up. He sat for a long time in the kitchen, in the dark, phone in hand. Ioana got up, found him there, and understood too, without him needing to speak. They wondered how to tell Rose-Hélène. They decided to wait until she woke up. But Rose-Hélène had woken up when she heard the phone. She was standing in the corridor in her pyjamas, and she had heard everything.

She didn’t cry straight away. She went up to her father, climbed onto his knees, and asked whether Antoine had said anything before he died. Julien repeated to her what the teacher had said. That Antoine had asked for water instead of flowers. That he had said she should be told. That she would know what to do. Rose-Hélène thought for a long time, her head against her father’s shoulder. Then she cried.

When she had finished crying, she said she knew what had to be done. They had to go to Corsica. Right away. For the funeral. And they had to bring water. Not just any water: water from La Duchère, from the fountain next to the lime tree. Julien tried to explain that it was far, that the funeral was in two days, that school… Ioana stopped him with a gesture. She said: “She’s right. We’re going.”

Isabelle came over from the other side of the landing as soon as she heard the news. She had never met Antoine. But she held Rose-Hélène in her arms for a long time, without a word, as she had on the day of her own mother’s death. Then she took a little bag of dried lime flowers out of her pocket, picked the previous summer in the Parc de la Tête d’Or. She gave it to Rose-Hélène to take to Corsica.

That evening, Yves Le Goff called from Brittany. He had heard the news from Nathalie. He talked for a long time with Julien, in his deep old sailor’s voice. He said he had never met Antoine, but he was sure Henri and he would have got on well: two stubborn men, two men of few words, two men who talked to things rather than to people. Then he asked to speak to Rose-Hélène. He told her to whistle loudly. So that it could be heard all the way to Brittany.

They left the next day, 13 March, on the night boat from Marseille. In her rucksack Rose-Hélène carried a one-litre bottle filled with water from the La Duchère fountain, which she had gone to fetch herself with Théo the evening before. Inès had come too, with her clarinet. She had told her lycée teachers she would be away for two days for family reasons. It wasn’t entirely untrue.

On the night boat, Rose-Hélène couldn’t sleep. She went up on deck with Inès, wrapped in a blanket. They looked at the black sea and the stars. Rose-Hélène asked Inès whether she was afraid of death. Inès thought for a long time. Then she said she had been afraid, before. But that since Odile’s farewell she thought death was a bit like the silence in the waltz. It was part of the music.

The village was waiting for them. It still looked devastated, with its black hills and half-burnt houses, but something had changed since August. The walls of the new school were beginning to rise next to the square, from Hugo’s plans. And on the wash-house wall there were still Rose-Hélène’s drawings, about thirty of them now, a little faded by the rain, held up with clothes pegs.

The youngest of the three singers came to meet them. Her name was Marie-Ange. She was seventy-one, with white hair pulled back in a bun and a peasant’s hands. She took Rose-Hélène in her arms without a word. Then she told her that in his last days Antoine had often talked about her. He said she would come in the spring. He said she had felt that the tree was alive. He said he believed her.

The night before the funeral, Antoine’s body was watched over all night in Marie-Ange’s house, according to Corsican tradition. The neighbours took turns around the coffin, two by two, until morning. Around midnight, the three singers sang a “lamentu”, a very ancient lament that Paul Santoni had only heard once in his life. Rose-Hélène fell asleep on her mother’s lap during the singing.

On the morning of the funeral, Ioana went to see the school building site. The workers were there, but they weren’t working. They had put down their tools and were waiting, in their Sunday best, to go to church. The site foreman showed Ioana where the stone bench would be, in front of the music room’s picture window. He said they had ordered it the day before from a stonemason in Corte. Antoine wouldn’t see it. But the tree would.

The funeral took place on 14 March, at eleven, in the little village church, then at the cemetery. The whole village was there, and people from Corte, and shepherds from the neighbouring mountains who had come on foot. As Antoine had asked, there were no flowers. Everyone carried a glass of water, a bottle, a jug. There were more than two hundred people. Nobody had ever seen a funeral like it.

In the church, the three women, of whom only two were singing because Marie-Ange didn’t have the strength, sang the same polyphonic song as on the day of the planting in June 2031. The priest spoke about Antoine. He said he had been a shepherd for eighty years, that he had never left his mountains except once, to see the sea at Ajaccio in 1962. He said he had watered a dead tree for eight months. Nobody smiled.

After the cemetery, the whole procession came back down to the square, in silence, each with their glass of water. The priest asked Rose-Hélène to begin. She walked up to the black tree, her La Duchère bottle in her hands. She poured the water at the foot of the trunk, slowly, as Dr Lefèvre had taught her. Then she stepped aside. And one after another, the two hundred villagers poured their water.

It took almost an hour. The earth around the tree turned black, then shiny, then a little puddle formed that reflected the grey sky. Rose-Hélène stood next to the tree the whole time, without moving, her empty bottle in her hand. When the last glass had been poured, she looked up at the branches. She looked at them for a long time, one by one, as Antoine used to look at them every morning.

There were no leaves. The branches were black and bare. It was still cold in March, at nine hundred metres. Julien went over to his daughter, afraid she would be disappointed. He told her gently that it was too early, that Dr Lefèvre had said they would have to wait until April, maybe May. Rose-Hélène didn’t answer. She walked around the tree, slowly, looking at every branch, her head raised.

Then she stopped. On the side that hadn’t burnt, the side she had touched in August, there was a low branch, barely taller than she was. At the end of that branch, so small you had to know it was there to see it, there was a bud. Just one. Brown, closed, swollen, the size of a grain of rice. Rose-Hélène looked at it without a word. Then she tugged at her father’s sleeve, as she had done under the La Duchère lime tree a year earlier.

Julien bent down. He saw the bud. He couldn’t believe his eyes. He called Marie-Ange, who came over leaning on her cane. Marie-Ange looked for a long time. Then she crossed herself. She said something in Corsican that Julien didn’t understand. The music teacher, who was standing nearby, translated: she had said that only yesterday morning there was nothing on that branch. She knew. She was the one who had watered it.

The news went round the square in seconds. People came closer, in silence, to see. Some were crying. Others were laughing. An old shepherd said out loud that Antoine had waited to leave so that the tree would make up its mind, because they were as stubborn as each other. Everyone laughed. Then the priest reminded them what Antoine had written in his letter to the little girl. The whole village knew the letter.

Rose-Hélène didn’t need reminding. She had already taken Henri’s harmonica out of her coat pocket. Antoine had written that if the tree had leaves, she should whistle the three notes to it, and it would know it was her. There were no leaves yet. There was a bud. Rose-Hélène decided that counted. She stood facing the low branch, very close to the bud. She closed her eyes.

She didn’t play. She whistled. As Antoine had asked. The first three notes of Henri’s waltz, off-key, with lots of air, in front of the bud, in front of two hundred people, in front of the black hills and the school under construction. Then she waited. And behind her, Inès raised her clarinet to her lips, Lucien Roux’s clarinet, and played the next three, very softly, almost in a murmur.

Then Marie-Ange, who hadn’t had the strength to sing in church, opened her mouth. She sang the rest of the waltz. Not with words: with her voice, the voice of an old Corsican woman, hoarse, deep, like no other. The other two singers joined her, one higher, the other lower. And the waltz of a Marseille sailor, born on a ship in Dakar in 1978, became a Corsican polyphonic song.

At the third verse, the three women stopped. Eight bars of silence, on the square, among the mountains. You could hear only the fountain, and the wind in the bare branches. Then, in that silence, someone whistled. It wasn’t Rose-Hélène. It was the old shepherd who had talked about stubbornness. Then another. Then a woman. Then a child. Then the whole village, two hundred people, whistled the end of the waltz together, off-key, magnificently off-key.

When the last whistle had died away, Rose-Hélène took Isabelle’s little bag out of her pocket. She opened it and scattered the dried lime flowers from the Tête d’Or on the wet earth at the foot of the Corsican tree. Flowers from Lyon for a tree in Corsica. She explained to Marie-Ange that they were the flowers of another lime tree, the one where a sailor had picked a flower in 1962, and that this way the two trees would know each other.

That evening, at Marie-Ange’s, they ate in silence, then talked a lot. Everyone had a story about Antoine. He had said one day in 1985 that he would never get on a plane, and he never had. He had told his wife in 1958 that he would love her to the end, and he had loved her for fifty years, until her death. And he had said last August that he would water the tree to the end. He had kept his word.

Marie-Ange took an envelope out of her apron. Antoine had entrusted it to her two weeks earlier, asking her to give it to the little girl from Lyon if she came. He had said she would come. The envelope contained just one thing: the old iron key to his sheepfold, in the mountains above the village. On the label, the teacher had written at his dictation: “For when you’re grown up. The sheep have gone, but the view has stayed.”

Rose-Hélène looked at the key for a long time. She now had three keys in her life: the one to Odile’s flat, on its blue ribbon, which she wore round her neck; the one to Nathalie’s attic room, which her mother kept in her pocket; and this one, the key to a sheepfold she had never seen. She asked Marie-Ange whether they could go up there. Marie-Ange said yes, but not today. Later. When she was grown up.

They stayed two more days in the village. Rose-Hélène went to see the bud every morning with Marie-Ange, and every morning she watered it with a little glass of water from the fountain. On the second morning she came running back: the bud had opened a little. Inside you could see a tip of green. A very tiny tip, smaller than a fingernail. But green. Marie-Ange said Antoine would have said it was spring.

On the last morning, Marie-Ange took Rose-Hélène to the little cemetery above the village. Antoine’s grave was very simple, a wooden cross and a mound of fresh earth. From there you could see the whole square, the fountain, the wash house, the school under construction and the black tree with its green branch. Rose-Hélène placed on the grave a drawing she had made the day before: a tree half green, half black, and an old man sitting on a bench, in the shade.

Before leaving, Rose-Hélène made Marie-Ange promise two things. First, that she would go on watering the tree every morning until it had all its leaves. Second, that she would send her a photo of the tree every week, just as Rose-Hélène had sent her drawings to Antoine. Marie-Ange promised. She said she didn’t know how to use a phone, but her grandson would show her. She kept her word too.

On the last night in the village, Rose-Hélène couldn’t sleep. Julien took her out to the square, under a sky full of stars such as you never see in the city. They sat on the edge of the fountain, opposite the tree. In the dark you couldn’t see the burnt side. You could only see the outline of the branches against the stars. Rose-Hélène said that like this the tree looked whole. Julien said that was perhaps how Antoine saw it.

On the boat home, Rose-Hélène fell asleep against Inès, Henri’s harmonica in one hand and the sheepfold key in the other. Julien and Ioana were on deck, in the cold wind, watching Corsica disappear into the night. Ioana asked Julien what Antoine had meant when he said the little girl would know what to do. Julien thought for a long time. Then he said Antoine had understood something before anyone else.

“He had understood that adults are afraid of death,” said Julien. “They don’t know what to say, what to do. They bring flowers, because they’ve been told they should bring flowers. Children don’t know you’re supposed to be afraid. So they do what seems logical to them. A tree is thirsty: you give it water. Someone has gone: you whistle so that they can hear.” Ioana took his hand. She said nothing.

Back in Lyon, Rose-Hélène told her class about the funeral. Mrs Chevalier had let her speak in front of everyone, sitting on the teacher’s little chair. She talked about the water, the bud, the village that whistled. The children listened without moving. At break, the whole class gathered around the silver lime in the playground. And Lucas, for the first time in his life, managed to whistle a note. Just one. For Antoine.

In Bucharest, Viorica heard the news from Ioana on the phone. She had never met Antoine either, but she had seen the video, like everyone. She asked for the village’s address to be sent to her. A week later, Marie-Ange received a letter from Romania, handwritten in French, in violet ink. Viorica had written that she too had waited a long time for something dead to come back to life. And that she knew it was worth it.

On 2 April, Marie-Ange sent the first spring photo. It showed the low branch, on the side that hadn’t burnt, covered in tiny tender-green leaves, about twenty of them. On 16 April, the second photo showed three branches covered in leaves. On 30 April, the whole left side of the tree was green. The right side, the one that had burnt, stayed black and bare. The tree looked like a face half in shadow, half in sunlight.

The day the first photo arrived, 2 April, Rose-Hélène did something she had been preparing for weeks. She opened the box of Henri’s harmonica, unfolded Antoine’s letter, and read it. All by herself. Aloud. Slowly, following the words with her finger, making two mistakes. Her parents listened from the doorway, not daring to breathe. When she had finished, she said: “There. Now I’ve read it myself.”

Dr Lefèvre, to whom Julien showed the photos, said it was exactly what she had hoped for. The tree would live. It would remain scarred, asymmetrical, with one side dead forever. But it would live, and in a few years new branches might grow on the burnt side. She added that she had never seen a lime tree survive such a fire. She asked what had been done to it. Julien answered: “We watered it. And we whistled to it.”

Amina, of course, had opened a spreadsheet for Marie-Ange’s photos. One row per week, with the date, the number of green branches and an estimate of the percentage of leaves. On 30 April she calculated that the tree had recovered forty-seven percent of its foliage. She showed the spreadsheet to Mr Vidal one Thursday evening. He checked the figures. They were right. He said forty-seven was almost half. Amina replied that it was exactly Antoine’s half.

That evening, Rose-Hélène wanted to dictate a letter for Antoine. Julien explained gently that Antoine wouldn’t be able to read it. She replied that she knew, but she wanted to write it anyway, and they would give it to Marie-Ange, who would read it to the tree. Julien took a pen. Rose-Hélène dictated four lines, like Antoine. She had counted. She wanted it to be fair.

“Dear Antoine, your tree has leaves. Half of them. The other half is for you. I whistled the three notes to it, and the whole village whistled the rest. It knew it was me. Rose-Hélène.” Julien copied the letter out neatly. Rose-Hélène signed it herself, in shaky capital letters, the first time she had written her whole first name. The article Corse-Matin published after Antoine’s funeral. A press article reports almost everything in indirect speech. Listen to the text twice, then read it aloud. At the end, answer 4 questions.
Le berger qui arrosait un arbre mort
Antoine, the shepherd whose video moved millions of people last summer, passed away on the night of 11 to 12 March, at the age of ninety-seven. Those close to him said he had gone peacefully.

According to the village mayor, Antoine had asked him the day before to organise a funeral without flowers. He had explained that he preferred everyone to bring water for the lime tree on the square, burnt during the July fire.
More than two hundred people respected his last wish on Tuesday. A neighbour told us she had never seen a funeral like it. “He had told us he would water to the end,” she added. “He kept his word.”
A little girl from Lyon poured the first water. Her father explained to us that Antoine had written her a letter in August, asking her to come back in the spring to see whether the tree had leaves.

That day, to everyone’s surprise, the child discovered a bud on a low branch. A villager assured us there had been nothing on that branch the day before. Dr Claire Lefèvre, a botanist in Lyon, confirmed the next day that the tree was alive.

The mayor announced that the new school, which would open in September, would have a stone bench facing the lime tree. He specified that it would be called “Antoine’s bench”, even though Antoine had stated, while alive, that it was ridiculous.

The summer I was fifteen, my grandfather took me fishing. That day he told me he wanted to talk to me about something important.
